absent: Interrupt translation table linear and two-level allocation layouts and entry formats
Translation service device table allocation sizes and interrupt translation table entry formats
Translation service enable and disable completion criteria
Generic polling helper timeouts, delays and atomic versus sleeping contexts
Routing service register accessor definitions and ordering guarantees
Global data layout including CPU interface width and priority storage

SPI range overlap handling across multiple routing instances

findings.text: Provides a trigger-mode configuration contract for shared peripheral interrupts: rising and falling are treated as one edge class, high and low as one level class, all other requests are rejected; successful updates are guarded so selection and mode programming appear atomic and are confirmed by hardware completion indications.

Exposes translation from logical CPU number to fabric affinity identifier with explicit validity tracking; uninitialised entries are reported as absent rather than returning a stale value, and registration binds a CPU to its owning routing service before enabling its processing element.

Offers lookup of the routing service owning a given shared interrupt number by range containment over a global list, and a global synchronisation operation issued through an arbitrary live instance with completion polling.

Second-level granule choice for the routing service is constrained jointly by operating system page size and advertised hardware support, preferring a native match and degrading deterministically; the result is always a supported encoding, never an unsupported request.

Translation table establishment requires an initially invalid table marker, derives usable identifier width from hardware minimum and maximum bounds further limited by processor interface capability and linear-table practicality, and selects flat versus hierarchical form using level support and a width threshold influenced by entry size and granule.

Translation service table shape requires advertised two-level support, prefers page-size-aligned granules with deterministic fallback to viable encodings, and abandons hierarchy when the granule address span would exceed the usable identifier width.

System-wide interrupt properties are captured once from the first routing service instance, relying on architectural consistency across instances, and include virtualisation capability, priority width, global shared-interrupt population and the shared logical-interrupt domain.
Register access for the translation service uses relaxed memory-mapped input-output through a per-instance base plus offset, with no stronger ordering implied by the accessor itself.
Completion polling macro forwards base, register and mask to a stringified helper, preserving register identity for diagnostics without changing polling semantics.

Shared-interrupt configuration state is protected by a per-instance raw spinlock held across the whole select-and-program transaction, preventing interleaving of selector updates and mode updates from different contexts.
Translation-service device bookkeeping is serialised by a per-node mutex initialised at node creation, separating device lifetime management from register access.
Per-CPU affinity record holds a sixteen-bit fabric identifier plus a boolean indicating whether the entry has been populated from firmware; consumers must check validity before use.

Routing-service lifecycle moves from allocation and register mapping through attribute programming and enable, firmware affinity capture, global-once initialisation and list linkage to operational; failure at an intermediate stage unwinds affinity, disables hardware and releases mapping and memory, and full teardown walks all instances while clearing affinity and domains.

Translation-service bring-up allocates a node, ensures prior disable if already active, programs memory attributes according to coherency, establishes device tables, enables hardware, then attaches its interrupt domain; each later failure reverses only the completed prefix.

Operational entries require prior discovery: global enable acts only on the first live routing service and fails when none exists or table establishment fails; CPU registration requires a valid affinity entry and an associated instance and validates selector acceptance before enabling the processing element.

Discovery entry scans firmware children for a specific compatibility identifier and attempts initialisation per match, reporting per-child failures without aborting the scan; the top-level probe dispatches between firmware-table modes.

Documented rejection modes include pre-validated translation tables, uninitialised or out-of-range affinity values, missing instance association, invalid selector acceptance, absent logical-interrupt support, firmware count mismatches, and mapping or allocation failures; these surface as distinct error indications and, where applicable, trigger unwind rather than partial operation.
Capability reporting uses single-bit indicators at bit eleven for four-kilobyte, bit twelve for sixteen-kilobyte and bit thirteen for sixty-four-kilobyte second-level granule support.

Priority width is conveyed as a small enumerated field mapping to one through five implemented bits with a safe one-bit default on reserved values; memory attributes form two coherent profiles, cacheable write-back inner-shareable versus non-cacheable with ignored shareability, applied consistently across translation, device and interrupt-table accesses.

Completion polling distinguishes transport idleness from logical validity: selector-based operations require both idle and a valid indication to succeed, while control operations require idle alone; idle without required validity is reported as an input-output failure distinct from polling failure.
